title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1 encoder renders the pre-release reasoning-effort budgets (high → 50; release reference and deepseek-recipe → 75)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/encoding_dsv41.py` (added in #39665) carries the pre-release reasoning-effort budget table, `low`/`high`/`xhigh` → 25/50/75. DeepSeek replaced that table on release day, so the prefix SGLang renders at index 0 of every thinking-mode V4.1 prompt no longer matches the model's own reference encoder or `deepseek-recipe`:

| source | low | high | xhigh | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` `encoding/encoding.py`, pre-release revision `fb2764a5` | 25 | 50 | 75 | 100 |
| same file from revision `df42c109` (2026-09-10) onward, current `dba1be0a` | 50 | 75 | — | 100 |
| `deepseek-recipe`, `deepseek-recipe-encoding/src/v4/dsv41.rs` (`reasoning_effort_template`) | 50 | 75 | 75 | 100 |
| SGLang main (`REASONING_EFFORT_MAPPINGS`, `encoding_dsv41.py` L68-73) | 25 | 50 | 75 | 100 |

Effect: a request with `reasoning_effort="high"`, or one that only switches thinking on and takes the server default (`high`), renders `Reasoning Effort: 50 (range 1-100, ...)` on SGLang while DeepSeek's reference and recipe render `Reasoning Effort: 75`; `low` renders 25 instead of 50. `max` is 100 in both tables, so evaluations run at `max` are unaffected. The model repository's `encoding/README.md` states the release mapping explicitly: `"low"` → 50, `"high"` → 75, `"max"` → 100, default `"high"`.

Apart from that line the SGLang encoder and the reference file agree byte-for-byte on the five cases under the model's `encoding/tests/` and on multi-turn, mid-conversation system, kept-reasoning and namespaced-tool conversations (checked with both modules side by side).

Expected: the table should follow the release reference (`low=50, high=75, max=100`); `xhigh` can stay as an alias of `high`, which is what `deepseek-recipe` renders for it. The cookbook sentence listing the tiers (`docs/cookbook/autoregressive/DeepSeek/DeepSeek-V4_1.mdx`) would want the budgets stated as well.

### Reproduction

```python
# ref = encoding/encoding.py downloaded from deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at revision dba1be0a
from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai import encoding_dsv41

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"},
]
print(ref.encode_messages(messages, thinking_mode="thinking", reasoning_effort="high")[:80])
# <｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜System｜>Reasoning Effort: 75 (range 1-100, the higher the value,
print(encoding_dsv41.encode_messages(messages, thinking_mode="thinking", reasoning_effort="high")[:80])
# <｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜System｜>Reasoning Effort: 50 (range 1-100, the higher the value,
```

Same result through the server: `reasoning_effort="high"` (or thinking on with no effort set) on `/v1/chat/completions` against `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` produces the 50 prefix.

### Environment

SGLang main at 923e4a56 (2026-09-17), Python 3.11, Linux x86_64; the rendering is pure string code and does not depend on GPU or kernels. Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (encoding file at revision `dba1be0a`).

title: [Feature] Unify the MoE router GEMM behind one gate layer
body:
## Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Motivation

Router GEMM precision is critical, and it matters most on long multi-turn work, where small differences accumulate over a long CoT. For example, in #29892 the routing precision change was worth +12.6pp resolved on swe-bench Verified (66.8% to 79.4%, 500 problems, GLM-5.2-FP8 on 4xGB300), even though the per-layer logit difference was only 2.6e-7 and single-layer top-k was bit-identical over 400 samples.

The precision that matters is in the output store. cuBLAS already accumulates a bf16 GEMM in fp32, so asking for fp32 output keeps the accumulator and costs nothing. For example, in #29783 we found that doing this on DSv3 moved accept length from 3.413 to 3.894.

Upcasting the activation as well is a much more expensive way to get there. In #29892 that path took 3 kernels at 16.7us per layer against 1 kernel at 8.7us, which over 93 MoE layers came out to 292 tok/s versus 327 tok/s, so -10.5% decode. That PR was closed once we agreed the bf16 GEMM with fp32 output gives the same effect.

Currently, every model in sglang implements its own version of this. For example, `deepseek_v2` has a six-way branch (AMX, deterministic, prefill-CP, tiny-gemm, aiter, cuBLAS), while `nemotron_h` and `minimax_m3` each open-code a bf16 matmul with fp32 output. Meanwhile GLM-4 MoE, `mimo_v2`, `laguna`, `hunyuan_v3`, `sarvam_moe` and `step3p5` still run the expensive activation upcast, so they are paying roughly what #29892 measured for an effect we can get for free. Similarly, `bailing_moe_v3` uses a triton matvec below M=8 and `deepseek_v2` uses tiny-gemm below M=16, so we have two thresholds and two kernels with slightly different numerics, and neither is shared.

Because of this, fixes do not propagate. `mimo_v2` was branched from `deepseek_v2` before #29783 landed, so it still casts the correction bias to bf16. `ernie4` and `kimi_linear` have the same problem, except unconditionally. And `bailing_moe`, `bailing_moe_linear` and `llada2` compute the router in fp32 and then cast the result straight back to bf16, which throws away the precision they just paid for. All of these wrote their own gate. K3 and K2.5 reuse deepseek's, so they picked up the fix for free.

We already have the kernels for this. #34693 already folded the DSv3 router kernel into the shared tiny GEMM for `deepseek_v2`, `dots3` and `kimi_k3`, so the kernel side is consolidating. The bf16 to fp32 GEMM helper in `kernels/ops/attention/dsv4/gemm.py` is also already a four-tier dispatcher (aiter, HPC bf16 split, DeepGEMM, cuBLAS). However, it lives under an attention directory named after one model, and longcat is the only model that opts into the HPC tier or tunes its threshold. Everyone else silently falls through to cuBLAS.

## Proposal

We should add a `RouterGate` layer next to `srt/layers/moe/topk.py` that always hands top-k fp32 logits, computed in bf16. The layer owns the kernel and the output dtype. This is also roughly what vLLM does, where the checkpoint config decides precision and the gate layer picks the kernel.

Deterministic inference should also be handled in the layer. Currently only `deepseek_v2` honors it for the router, so for example `bailing_moe_v3` still switches kernel at small token counts with no guard, and the same token can route differently depending on batch size even with the flag on.

As part of this we should move the bf16 to fp32 GEMM helper out of the DSv4 attention directory, since the router is its main consumer, and move the small-token-count threshold helper out of `models/deepseek_common/`. It currently lives in a model package, which is probably why bailing wrote its own.

Independent of the refactor, there are also three small fixes we can land now: drop the bf16 correction bias in `mimo_v2`, `ernie4` and `kimi_linear`, and drop the cast back to bf16 in `bailing_moe`, `bailing_moe_linear` and `llada2`.

## Benefits

- Every model gets fp32 router logits at the cost of the bf16 GEMM.
- A router numerics fix lands in one place and applies everywhere.
- The HPC and DeepGEMM tiers become available to every model.
- The small-token-count path has one threshold and one kernel.

## Related resources

- #29783, the original DSv3 router fix
- #29892, where we measured the activation upcast and closed it in favor of this approach
- #31001, #31502 and #31927, where the bf16 bias cast was re-added and then removed again after the FlashInfer 0.6.15 bump
- #34693, which replaced the DSv3 router GEMM with the unified tiny GEMM
- Megatron-LM's routing precision change for fine-grained MoE: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/commit/dab7723821fc326564634b398a809d43740a6c8d
- A recent silent-downcast fix in their ModelOpt example: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/pull/5810
- vLLM's `GateLinear`: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/router/gate_linear.py

title: [Bug] Anthropic `/v1/messages`: prior-turn thinking is spliced into content, which breaks the Qwen3.8 chat template (empty `<think>` + inline `<think>…</think>`); model starts emitting `</think>` as visible text
body:
### Environment

- SGLang v0.5.19 (the relevant code is unchanged in v0.5.20 and `main` as of 2026-09-23)
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4 checkpoint whose `chat_template.jinja` is byte-identical to the official one)
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- Client: Claude Code over `/v1/messages`. It sends prior assistant `thinking` blocks back on every turn.

### What happens

`anthropic/serving.py` → `_convert_assistant_thinking_blocks()`:

- `supports_native_reasoning_history()` returns `chat_encoding.spec_owns_reasoning_history(spec)`, which is `spec is not None`. That makes it **False for every HF/Jinja-template model**.
- So the prior thinking goes through `wrap_reasoning_history()` and is spliced into the assistant **content** as `<think>{R}\n</think>`.

The Qwen3.8 template reads **only** `message.reasoning_content`, and `preserve_thinking` is on by default. It therefore renders every prior assistant turn like this (output of `tokenizer.apply_chat_template`):

```
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>

</think>

<think>{previous reasoning}
</think>{text}

<tool_call>…
```

Expected, when the same history is passed as `reasoning_content`:

```
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>
{previous reasoning}
</think>

{text}

<tool_call>…
```

Why this used to be harmless: the Qwen3.5/3.6 templates had a fallback, `{%- if '</think>' in content %}`, that pulled inline reasoning back out of the content. **The Qwen3.8 template dropped that fallback.**

### Observed effect

The model imitates the pattern "two `</think>` per turn" and emits a second `</think>` in visible text, just before its tool call.

| Claude Code session | thinking echoed | assistant text blocks | blocks containing `</think>` |
|---|---|---|---|
| long agentic run (~4 h) | yes | 212 | **14** |
| long agentic run (~8 h) | yes | 319 | **7** |
| runs where no thinking was echoed (blocks empty or absent) | no | 853 | **0** |

This is exactly what the docstring of `spec_owns_reasoning_history` predicts: *"Splicing a detector's markers into content instead nests a reasoning block inside the content channel and leaves the real one empty, teaching the model to emit raw markers as visible text."*

PR #35480 kept Jinja models on the splice because *"their markers really do live in the content stream"*. That holds for templates with the fallback. It does not hold for Qwen3.8.

### Suggested fix

For HF templates that consume `reasoning_content`, pass the history through the native path that custom encoders already use. A minimal version:

```python
# anthropic/serving.py, _convert_assistant_thinking_blocks
template = self._chat_template() or ""
if self.openai_serving_chat.supports_native_reasoning_history() or "reasoning_content" in template:
    return reasoning_text, None
```

We checked that the `/v1/chat/completions` path carries `reasoning_content` into this template correctly. We replayed a real 40K-token Claude Code request both ways:

- The spliced form was 40,442 prompt tokens and the `reasoning_content` form was 40,424.
- The difference is the same when the prompt is rendered directly with the tokenizer.
- The rendered text shows the expected format.

For comparison, vLLM's Anthropic endpoint maps prior `thinking` blocks to `reasoning` / `reasoning_content`.

### What we are *not* claiming

- **We have not measured the impact on output quality.** The only effect we measured is the leaked marker.
- **It is not the cause of long thinking turns.** We replayed the same real request 4× per variant with `max_tokens=16000`. The spliced form hit the cap 4/4 times; the `reasoning_content` form hit it 3/4 times.

Happy to test a patch on our setup (DGX Spark, 8 concurrent Claude Code users).

title: [Perf] DeepSeek-V4 dsv4 prefill on SM120 (4x RTX PRO 6000, TP=4): ~2-7K tok/s vs ~12.5K reported via vLLM/marlin on identical hardware — expected? tuning guidance?
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched existing issues; found SM120 kernel-coverage work (#19637 roadmap, #30272) but nothing on dsv4-backend prefill throughput specifically.
- [x] English.

### Question / observation

DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120, 96 GB, TP=4, PCIe gen5, no NVLink), sglang v0.5.16, `dsv4` attention backend, `flashinfer_mxfp4` MoE, fp8_e4m3 KV: **prefill throughput sits at ~2-7K tok/s**, while a stock **vLLM 0.25.1 recipe on identical hardware reports ~12.5K tok/s prefill at 256K context** (marlin MoE backend, expert parallelism, fp8 KV — https://github.com/hermia-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-sm120-stock-vllm). A 4-6× gap at large context on the same GPUs suggests the SM120 dsv4 prefill path has significant headroom. Is this expected/known, and is there tuning guidance?

### Our measurements (sglang v0.5.16 + the #33407 dispatch fix, DSPARK enabled)

- Aggregate prefill, 9 concurrent ~90K-token prompts: **~5,540 tok/s** (813K prompt tokens / 146.9 s wall; outputs negligible at 61 tokens each)
- Aggregate prefill, 3 concurrent ~650K-token prompts: **~2,805 tok/s** (1.95M / 695.5 s)
- Single ~650K-token prompt: **~2,870 tok/s** (226.4 s to first token)
- Live scheduler logs show per-batch input throughput starting ~6.5K tok/s at low sequence position and declining to ~1.8-2.1K past several hundred K tokens (attention cost growth expected — but the absolute level is the question)
- `--chunked-prefill-size` 4096 vs 8192: statistically identical wall time (146.9 vs 149.0 s on the 9×90K test), so chunking overhead isn't the limiter
- Startup notes `Breakable CUDA graph is incompatible with DeepSeek-V4 (heavy capture-pool memory pressure); disabling prefill CUDA graph` — so DSV4 prefill runs graph-less on this path
- `--max-prefill-tokens` at default 16384; `--disable-flashinfer-autotune` set (SM120 autotune instability, upstream rec)

### Relevant config

```
--tp-size 4 --trust-remote-code
--mem-fraction-static 0.90 --context-length 1048576
--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.1
--max-running-requests 64 --cuda-graph-max-bs 64
--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4
--speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-attention-mode decode
--disable-custom-all-reduce --chunked-prefill-size 4096
--disable-flashinfer-autotune
```

(`--disable-custom-all-reduce` because sgl_kernel custom allreduce fails CUDA-graph capture on our PCIe GPU pairs, #11957 class.)

### Questions

1. Is dsv4-backend prefill on SM120 known to be unoptimized relative to the decode path (which benchmarks well for us — ~1,280 out tok/s at concurrency 64 with DSPARK)?
2. The vLLM recipe uses expert parallelism (`--enable-expert-parallel`) and the marlin MoE backend. Would `--ep-size 4` (or an EP/TP hybrid) be expected to materially improve MoE prefill on PCIe-only SM120 boxes with sglang, and is that combination supported with `flashinfer_mxfp4`?
3. Is the disabled prefill CUDA graph a meaningful contributor at these chunk sizes, or is the gap dominated by MoE GEMM kernel choice on SM120?
4. Any recommended experiments/flags for prefill specifically on this hardware class? Happy to run and report numbers — SM120 hardware is available for validation.

Context: prefill throughput directly bounds a fairness problem we've documented (a single large-context prefill monopolizes chunked-prefill admission for its full duration — several minutes at ~2K tok/s for near-1M prompts — starving concurrent small requests).

title: [Tracking] Upstream remaining sglang-miles changes to main
body:
Track the remaining work to land on `main`. **Source PRs are already merged into miles branches; they are references, not pending PRs.**

## Status guide

| Main PR / next action | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A PR link only | Existing main PR, open at the last check. Advance it. |
| **Create/link main PR** | No upstream PR is linked in this tracker. Link an existing PR or create one. |
| **Decide / link PR** or **Decide: …** | First confirm whether main still needs the change; then port, revise, or drop it. |
| **Partial; …** or **Related PR; …** | Existing PR coverage is partial or unconfirmed. Identify and complete the remaining work. |
| **Reconcile …** | Overlapping proposals or later fixes need to be aligned before proceeding. |
| **Include in on-policy port** | This fix depends on the on-policy feature and should be delivered with it. |
| **Assign an internal coordinator** | An internal maintenance owner still needs to be assigned. |

Each work item has one checkbox. The handle beside each PR is its GitHub PR author. **Ownership: internal PR author first; otherwise, the maintainer who merged that PR (`mergedBy`).** For an unmerged external main PR, the corresponding Source PR owner coordinates upstreaming. Reviewer and commit identity do not determine ownership. If there is no Source PR or verified merger, leave ownership unassigned. External authors are not pinged.

title: [Feature] EFA SGLang  image should work out of the box on AWS NVIDIA GPUs (NIXL & Mooncake)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Currently on pytorch images, there is  automatic AWS EFA & auto gcp nccl plugin detection & setup such that efa & gcp networks work out of the box. [source: https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/frameworks/pytorch-release-notes/rel-26-07.html ] 

Unfortunately on SGLang images, using NIXL EFA & Mooncake EFA requires an massive undocumented script to download the correct EFA userspace libraries. (related workstream in vLLM community in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55783  )

Any chance that EFA NIXL  & EFA mooncake can work out of the box on SGLang too?

For NIXL, it requires manually installing the efa userspace libs in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile.cu134 

For Mooncake it requires uninstalling `mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13` preinstalled in the image and then installing `mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13==0.3.13.post1` , `mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13` itself does not work with SGLang yet  then following this gaint list of instructions. Note that these list of instructions is only valdiated on nightly containers and not in current `0.5.20` release container yet

instructions from sglang community in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39973

```
On an x86_64 AWS EFA instance, replace the standard CUDA 13 Mooncake package with the EFA build. The two packages install the same `mooncake` Python module, so do not install them side by side.

The following commands replace the package in an SGLang CUDA 13 environment while preserving its existing Python dependencies:

python3 -m pip uninstall -y \
  mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13 \
  mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13
python3 -m pip install --no-deps \
  mooncake-transfer-engine-efa-cuda13==0.3.13.post1

export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/opt/amazon/efa/lib:/opt/amazon/efa/lib64:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
export MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL=efa

python3 -c 'from mooncake import engine; assert engine.SUPPORT_EFA'
fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM

The EFA wheel expects a compatible AWS EFA userspace installation on the host and does not bundle `libfabric` or `libefa`. The current wheel is available only for x86_64. It is built without Mooncake EP/PG and the NVLink/MNNVL components, so use the standard Mooncake CUDA package for those features.

The current libfabric EFA provider cannot transfer CUDA VMM-backed buffers. Until [libfabric issue #12853](https://github.com/ofiwg/libfabric/issues/12853) is resolved, apply these settings to both prefill and decode workers:

- Do not set `SGLANG_MOONCAKE_CUSTOM_MEM_POOL` to `NVLINK` or `BAREX`.
  `INTRA_NODE_NVLINK` is supported because it uses the default CUDA allocator.
- Do not enable `expandable_segments:True` in `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF` or `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF`.
- Post-capture KV sizing is automatically disabled for the EFA protocol because
  its KV cache uses CUDA VMM allocations.
- Do not set `MC_FORCE_MNNVL` or `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE`; EFA is not an MNNVL transport.

SGLang validates the first two constraints at startup to avoid a later `fi_read` or `fi_write` failure from libfabric.
```

title: [Feature] Incremental chat-prompt processing: stop re-tokenizing the whole history on every turn
body:
## Problem

A multi-turn chat request re-sends the entire conversation. On every turn `OpenAIServingChat` re-renders the chat template over all messages and re-encodes the full rendered prompt, on the TokenizerManager's event loop, before the request reaches the scheduler. Prefix caching already makes the *prefill* of the repeated history nearly free, but this CPU work still grows with every turn and becomes the part of time to first token that grows with history.

On Gemma 4 26B-A4B (1x H100, SGLang v0.5.18), rendering took 23.0 ms and encoding 11.8 ms at 301 messages. That cost is paid serially per request, so under concurrency it also queues requests behind each other on the tokenizer loop.

## Measurement

We replayed PIPPA character-chat conversations ([`PygmalionAI/PIPPA`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PygmalionAI/PIPPA)): recorded human turns in order, with the model writing the other side. This ran at 16 concurrent streams on 1x H100 with 1,738 identical requests per arm, both arms running at the same time on one box, and zero errors. It compared stock SGLang against an out-of-tree plugin that reuses the previous turn's rendered text and token ids:

| | stock | incremental | speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| TTFT p50 | 417.4 ms | 275.6 ms | 1.52x |
| TTFT p90 | 689.7 ms | 414.9 ms | 1.66x |
| TTFT p99 | 805.0 ms | 494.2 ms | 1.63x |
| decode tok/s per stream | 70.6 | 75.3 | |

The gain scales with history length, which is the signature of the mechanism: 1.00x at 0-2K prompt tokens, 1.45x at 2-4K, 1.50x at 4-6K, 1.54x at 6-8K, 1.71x at 8-10K, 1.69x at 10-12K and 1.72x at 12-15K. There is nothing to reuse when there is no history, and the null result at 0-2K shows the effect is not drift.

**Correctness:** prompt token ids were identical between arms on 205/205 turns checked via `return_prompt_token_ids`.

Note: this run enabled both halves of the plugin, incremental template *rendering* (a Gemma 4-specific renderer) and incremental *tokenization*. The linked PR upstreams the tokenization half, which is model-agnostic.

## Proposal

1. **Incremental tokenization (model-agnostic, PR attached).** Cache the token ids of recently seen histories. For a new request, find the longest cached history whose messages are a prefix of the new messages and whose rendered text is a prefix of the new render. Encode only the new text and append it at a boundary where concatenation is provably identical to a full encode: the appended text must begin with a special added token that strips no whitespace. Anything else falls back to a full encode. Opt-in flag, default off.
2. **Incremental rendering (follow-up, open question).** Jinja re-walks every message on every request. Reusing a rendered prefix is only safe for templates whose output is append-only. That property can be probed and verified per template, but some templates re-render earlier turns (e.g. stripping reasoning from old assistant turns). Would maintainers prefer this in the Python path, or in the new Rust renderer?

Separately, Gemma 4's own `chat_template.jinja` renders in time quadratic in message count, because of a per-message forward scan. A linear, byte-identical fix has been proposed on the model repo: https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it/discussions/66

title: [RFC] Explicit, budgeted tail-replay for Mamba/GDN state in UnifiedRadixCache
body:
**Update 2026-09-24**: real-server A/B + e2e fidelity experiments done (Qwen3.8-27B hybrid, 2×910B3). Conclusion up front: **the retreat scenario is real and large (93% of requests, 30% of prefill compute), but both candidate replay mechanisms are economically unviable on interleaved hybrids — the correct lever is checkpoint placement/retention policy in the existing engine, not a new execution path.** Details and tables below. Instrumentation: #41001.

**Area**: `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/` (UnifiedRadixCache, MambaComponent, schedule_batch) · Related: #37424, #37795, #37091–#37914, #39115, #28511, #38652

## Problem

On hybrid models, when the Mamba checkpoint behind a full-KV hit is missing or evicted, the engine retreats the whole hit to that checkpoint and re-prefills the gap through all layers — even though the gap's full-KV is already cached.

## A/B results (150-request agentic traces per cell, first-admission semantics)

**1. Where the problem lives — retreat rate by pressure type**

| Pressure | Requests retreating (H > C) | Gap (H−C) p50 / max | Replay-eligible tokens | TTFT p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (control) | 0% | — | 0 | 2.5s |
| full-KV capacity (112K) | **0%** (whole nodes evicted, `H == C`) | — | 0 | 46.4s |
| Mamba pool = 48 | 0% | — | 0 | 2.5s |
| Mamba pool = 32 | 4% | 22K / 50K | 156K | 2.5s |
| Mamba pool = 24 | 79% | 32K / 50K | 3.53M | — |
| Mamba pool = 16 | **93%** | 32K / 49K | **4.12M** | 49.3s |
| 12 sessions, pool = 32 | 92% | 25K / 66K | 7.88M | — |
| 12 sessions, pool = 16 | 96% | 16K / 49K | 8.16M | — |

→ The problem requires **Mamba pool pressure**, not full-KV pressure: full-KV eviction removes whole nodes (`H == C` by construction) and hides the gap entirely.

**2. What the retreat costs — avoidable compute** (modeled from measured TTFT grids; "avoided" = if every winnable gap were repaired)

| Cell | Gap tokens to repair | Modeled re-prefill time | Avoided compute |
|---|---|---|---|
| mb32 | 156K | 314s → 301s | **4.3%** |
| mb24 | 3.53M | 875s → 608s | **30.5%** |
| mb16 (seed 0) | 4.12M | 1422s → 973s | **31.6%** |
| mb16 (seed 1) | 3.84M | 914s → 624s | **31.7%** |
| mb16 (seed 2) | 3.99M | 940s → 644s | **31.5%** |
| 12 sessions, pool 32 | 7.88M | 1885s → 1310s | **30.5%** |
| 12 sessions, pool 16 | 8.16M | 1891s → 1318s | **30.3%** |

**3. Output fidelity — e2e greedy continuation, 32 tokens** (noise floor = flush-cache fresh-vs-fresh)

| Tier | Setup | Exact match | Mean match |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise floor | two fresh prefills, cache flushed | **28/28** | 32/32 |
| Leaf-checkpoint seed | clean full hit, GDN from donated state | **14/20** | diverge ≤ 23 tok |
| Aged-checkpoint replay | retreat to checkpoint C < H | env-sensitive* | — |

\* Instrumented state diff confirms the mechanism: divergence occurs iff the seed position ≠ the reference's live position; same-position seeds are 100% token-identical. Two upstream-facing findings: (a) track placement is nondeterministic across identical runs (same prompt: 2816 / 2688 / none), (b) GDN state numerics are chunk-decomposition sensitive. Both already affect today's clean-hit path.

## Why replay is economically unviable here (corrects the original proposal)

Qwen3.5 interleaves GGGF (48 GDN + 16 FA): every GDN layer consumes the previous layer's output.

| Candidate mechanism | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| Split-prefix extend (FA at `H`, GDN replays `[C, P)`) | Once FA skips `[C, H)`, later GDN layers have no hidden states to replay with. Running FA over `[C, H)` anyway costs the same as today — **saving zero**. |
| ReplaySSM-style ring reconstruction (#28511) | Ring records ≈ 0.8 MB/token across 48 layers → covering a measured 32K gap costs **~25 GB per request**, vs ~13s of re-prefill compute. **Memory cost exceeds the compute it avoids by orders of magnitude.** |

The corollary: today's retreat (all-layer re-prefill of `[C, P)`) is already compute-optimal for this architecture — every FLOP in it is necessary. The waste is not in *how* the gap is repaired but in *that the gap exists at all*.

## Revised proposal

1. **Observability (land now)**: first-admission retreat metrics — `mamba_retreat_requests_total`, `mamba_retreat_gap_tokens_total`, `mamba_retreat_collapse_requests_total`, gap histogram, `mamba_replay_would_admit_total`. Working implementation + unit tests on fork branch `rfc40865-phase1-retreat-metrics` (instrumentation in #41001). This lets every deployment quantify its own retreat rate before any policy change.
2. **Checkpoint retention policy (the real lever)**: keep the gap small instead of repairing it — pin the most recent K checkpoints per active session (78 MB/slot at this model size, so pinning K=4 for 100 sessions ≈ 31 GB — a tunable trade vs 30% re-prefill), and/or use a denser track interval for active sessions so `C` tracks `H` closely. The engine already self-heals via force-track at the branching point (`_force_track_h`); under pool pressure those healing checkpoints get evicted, which is what turns one retreat into a persistent collapse — retention targets exactly that.
3. **Replay execution path: withdrawn.** Both mechanisms fail economically (table above). Keeping this RFC open as the measurement record for findings (a)/(b).

## Asks

1. OK to land the first-admission retreat metrics upstream (item 1)?
2. Interest in the checkpoint retention policy (item 2) — and where should it live: MambaComponent eviction ordering vs scheduler-side pinning?
3. Are findings (a) track-placement nondeterminism and (b) chunk-decomposition-dependent GDN numerics worth separate upstream issues? Happy to file with the measurement protocol and data.

title: [RFC] SGLang renderer
body:
Tracking what is still missing. Landed with #36718, which covers `/chat` and `/completions` in standalone and serving modes.

## Gaps

| # | Category | Item | Issue | PR | Status |
| - | -------- | ---- | ----- | -- | ------ |
| 1 | CI | Publish renderer image | — | [#40639](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40639) | ✅ Done |
| 2 | Cleanup | Deduplicate preprocessing logic | — | #40609 </br> #40781 | 🚧 WIP |
| 3 | Decode | Delegate decode to renderer | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 4 | Decode | Stop strings detection | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 5 | Protocol | Stateless `/responses` | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 6 | Protocol | `/messages` | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 7 | Protocol | `/detokenize` | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 8 | Cleanup | Delegate tokenizer instantiation to the renderer | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 9 | MM | Multimodal support without pixel values creation | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 10 | Protocol | Stateful `/responses` support | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 11 | Transport | gRPC support | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 12 | Parsers | Own reasoning and tool parsers | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 13 | Cleanup | Delegate the server's OpenAI routes into the renderer | — | — | ⬜ TBD |
| 14 | Serve | Native sidecar support in `sglang serve` | — | — | ⬜ TBD |

## Open questions

- Rust server boundaries: should the rust frontend only take token ids in and out, leaving everything before and after to the renderer?
- Client or proxy: does the frontend call the renderer, or does the renderer sit in front? In the proxy shape the frontend never knows, it only ever sees rendered `GenerateRequest`s.
- Do we need shared `sglang-protocols` crates for the wire types, or can we just keep them in the renderer crate?
- Stop strings is the only(?) case where the rust frontend needs to be aware of the textual representation of token-ids. In case the rust frontend becomes TITO, where should that component sit, and how the rust server interacts with it every turn?

## Notes

1. HTTP and grpc wire types stay dumb DTOs. Boundary mapping lowers them to protocol structs, where the logic lives (following #36923).
2. New endpoints don't need their own version of chat. They lower to it, the way python's anthropic layer already does.
3. Media crosses as ids and hashes, and the heavy tensors can be built later where they are needed.

## References

* [Disaggregated request preprocessing (design RFC)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/28669)
* [Non-GPU process rust migration (wider context)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/23206)

title: [Feature] Support configurable retention for request log files
body:
## Checklist

- [x] This is a feature request, not a general usage question.
- [x] This issue is written in English.

## Motivation

When running SGLang as a long-lived service with `--log-requests` and a file target configured through `--log-requests-target`, request log archives can accumulate and consume increasing disk space. I would like to configure how long these files are retained through a server startup argument.

In the checkout I inspected, `python/sglang/srt/utils/log_utils.py` creates a `TimedRotatingFileHandler` with `when="H"` and `backupCount=0`. This rotates files hourly but does not remove old archives. I could not find a request-log retention-days CLI option or an existing issue directly tracking this requirement.

### Proposed behavior

Add an optional argument such as `--log-requests-retention-days` (proposed name, not an existing option):

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <MODEL_PATH> \
  --log-requests \
  --log-requests-level 3 \
  --log-requests-format json \
  --log-requests-target /var/log/sglang/requests \
  --log-requests-retention-days 7
```

- Retain request log archives for a configurable number of days and delete archives older than that time window.
- Preserve the existing unlimited-retention behavior when the option is omitted.
- Apply time-based expiration rather than approximating retention with a fixed number of backup files: keeping 168 hourly archives is not necessarily equivalent to keeping seven days of logs when traffic is intermittent.
- Check for expired archives at startup and periodically during runtime, including when no requests arrive. A documented cleanup interval is acceptable; exact-to-the-second deletion is not required.
- Limit cleanup to archives owned by the current logging instance and leave active logs and unrelated files untouched. Cleanup across previous instances or old Pods sharing a directory should be an explicit, separate policy.

The primary request is configurable retention. Configurable rotation frequency can be discussed separately and is not required for this feature.

### Validation expectations

Focused tests should verify that expired archives are removed, unexpired archives and active files are preserved, unrelated/other-instance files are not deleted, and cleanup also works at startup and during idle periods.

## Related resources

- Request log file-target support: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/16338
- Request logger: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/utils/request_logger.py
- File handler setup: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/utils/log_utils.py

I would like to contribute an implementation and would appreciate feedback on the CLI name and retention/cleanup semantics before proceeding.

title: [diffusion] Make warmup preferred preload components and headroom configurable
body:
## Motivation

Follow-up from [#40562](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/40562) / [#40761](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40761).

PR #40761 fixes the immediate warmup OOM by:

1. Skipping preferred preload when host weights do not fit free device memory (with a fixed 1 GiB margin), and recovering from mid-copy OOM.
2. Not prefetching unused same-stage experts (e.g. `transformer_2`) at stage exit.

Two related policy gaps remain:

### Preferred preload is not user-configurable

`preferred_ready_after_request` is hard-coded in stage `ComponentUse` declarations. Users cannot:

- disable all warmup preferred preloads;
- explicitly select which components to keep ready after warmup;
- configure the memory headroom used by the budget check (`_WARMUP_PRELOAD_MARGIN_BYTES` is fixed at 1 GiB).

The current weight-only budget check also does not reserve room for activations / attention workspaces on the first real request, so a component can pass the preload check and still OOM shortly after.

### Proposal

Expose a user-facing policy, for example:

```text
--warmup-preload-components auto|none|<comma-separated-list>
```

- `auto` (default): keep today's `preferred_ready_after_request` behavior
- `none`: skip all preferred warmup preloads
- explicit list (e.g. `text_encoder,dit`): only preload the named components

Optionally also:

```text
--warmup-preload-margin-gib <float>
```

to override the fixed 1 GiB headroom.

## Related

- Issue: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/40562
- PR: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40761

title: penalties use one step stale history under the overlap scheduler
body:
with the overlap scheduler on (default), frequency, presence and repetition penalties are applied to `[prompt[-1]] + output[:i-1]` when sampling output token `i` instead of `output[:i]`. with `--disable-overlap-schedule` they use `output[:i]` as expected.

`ScheduleBatch.cumulate_penalty_output_tokens` (python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_batch.py) takes `req.output_ids[-1]` or `req.origin_input_ids[-1]` before any output while the next decode step is being prepared. under overlap the previous step's token is still in flight at that point so req.output_ids lags by one. the first decode step penalises the last prompt token and each later step adds the token from two steps back

how I checked: greedy requests with one penalty each (`frequency_penalty=1.0`, `presence_penalty=1.0`, `repetition_penalty=1.3`), 16 prompts * 32 tokens, SGLang 0.5.20, SmolLM2-135M-Instruct in float16, one A100. every returned logprob was compared with a float32 Hugging Face recompute under both histories (mean / max absolute difference):

| | overlap on, `output[:i]` | overlap on, `[prompt[-1]] + output[:i-1]` | overlap off, `output[:i]` |
|---|---|---|---|
| frequency | 0.018 / 0.52 | 0.002 / 0.013 | 0.002 / 0.013 |
| presence | 0.015 / 0.52 | 0.002 / 0.014 | 0.002 / 0.015 |
| repetition | 0.18 / 7.17 | 0.002 / 0.014 | 0.002 / 0.014 |

The 0.002 / 0.014 cells are float16 noise, so under overlap the shifted history is the one that matches.

Effect: the last prompt token gets penalized, which matters when it's a token the model wants to continue with (a space or newline), and every new token is penalized one step late.

The code is unchanged on main (ce06a1444). Probe script: https://github.com/iemAnshuman/baton/blob/main/baton/backends/sglang_penalty_probe.py

title: [Bug] Cache request finalization is tied to cache_finished_req: aborted LMCache sessions can leak
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at [https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions). Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

> Line numbers below are from `174a5f37b9` and drift quickly; each reference also names the
> enclosing function so it stays findable.

## Summary

`LMCRadixCache` does not implement `release_aborted_request`, so aborts fall through to the
no-op default in `BasePrefixCache` (`base_prefix_cache.py:371`):
```python
def release_aborted_request(self, handle: CacheRequestHandle) -> None:
    """Release attempt state; caches without prefetch state have nothing to drop."""
```

Nothing raises, so the gap is silent.

In MP mode, `LMCRadixCache.match_prefix` opens an LMCache session and may leave a pending
lookup holding daemon-side read locks; `init_load_back` is what consumes them. A request
aborted between those two points leaks, for the lifetime of the server:

- `_mp_load_back_markers[rid]`, recorded in `_mp_match_prefix` (`lmc_radix_cache.py:231`) and
  consumed in `init_load_back` (`:303`);
- the connector-side pending lookup;
- daemon-side read locks, which block eviction of the entries they cover;
- an LMCache session that never receives `END_SESSION`.

Flushing the cache does not recover any of it. `LMCRadixCache.reset` (`lmc_radix_cache.py:173`)
clears the local marker dict but never calls `end_session`, so the daemon-side session and its
locks survive until the process exits.

The straightforward fix — calling `end_session(handle.rid)` from `release_aborted_request` — is
**not safe in general**, and the abort hook also cannot simply be moved later, because another
backend depends on the current ordering. Details below.

Related closed PR (not merged): #40334, closed by me after finding the ordering problem.

## Analysis

### Why the obvious fix is unsafe

On current main there are thirteen places where an abort reaches the cache layer: ten via
`Scheduler._release_aborted_request` (`scheduler.py:3239`, `:3249`, `:3257`, `:3340`, `:3556`,
`:5429`, `:5456`, `:5476`, and `disaggregation/prefill.py:1129`, `:1555`) and three that call
`finish(handle, CacheRequestOutcome.ABORT)` directly (`prefill.py:1170` in
`handle_bootstrap_failure`'s caller path, `:1201` in `handle_bootstrap_failure`, and
`decode_hicache_mixin.py:190` in `_clean_hicache_prefetch_resources`).

Four of them (`scheduler.py:3239`, `:3249`, `:3257`, `:3340` — retire-unadmitted, queue-limit
rejection, and priority preemption) never reach `cache_finished_req` at all, so for those the
abort hook is the only possible cleanup point. `prefill.py:1201` performs no KV release either.

The rest do reach it via `release_kv_cache` (`common.py:280`). Most notably the
disaggregated-decode waiting-queue abort passes the default `is_insert=True`:
```text
scheduler.py:5429   _release_aborted_request(req)
scheduler.py:5438   release_kv_cache(req, self.tree_cache)      # is_insert=True
                      -> LMCRadixCache.cache_finished_req
                         -> store_kv       (lmc_radix_cache.py:489)
                         -> end_session    (lmc_radix_cache.py:493)
```

Adding `end_session` to the abort hook turns that into `end_session -> store_kv -> end_session`.

That relies on the external LMCache implementation treating `end_session` as idempotent.
SGLang declares no `lmcache` dependency at all (it is not in `python/pyproject.toml`), so that
contract is unpinned and unverifiable from this repository. It also permits a STORE after the
session has been closed — and MP `store_kv` blocks until the daemon signals, per the comment at
`lmc_radix_cache.py:490` — so the failure mode is not necessarily a silent no-op.

Tracking active sessions inside SGLang would prevent the second call, but cannot fix the
ordering: the first `end_session` still precedes the STORE.

### Why the abort hook cannot simply be moved later

Backends differ in whether they tolerate running abort cleanup after `cache_finished_req`:

- `UnifiedRadixCache` does override `cache_finished_req` (`unified_radix_cache.py:953`), but it
  does not touch the prefetch, linker or buffer-pipeline state cleaned by its
  `release_aborted_request` (`:2587`) — order-independent.
- `FlexKVRadixCache` **requires the current order**. Its `cache_finished_req`
  (`flexkv_radix_cache.py:388`) may `inc_lock_ref` a source node, launch an async store on
  `store_stream`, and register it:
  ```python
  # flexkv_radix_cache.py:447
  with self._node_lock:
      self._inflight_store_nodes[req.cache_request_handle] = new_last_node
  ```
  while `release_aborted_request` (`:488`) pops that registration and releases the lock:
  ```python
  with self._node_lock:
      node = self._inflight_store_nodes.pop(handle, None)
  if node is not None:
      self.dec_lock_ref(node)
  ```
  Running cleanup afterwards would drop the lock of a store still in flight, letting eviction
  free its source slots — exactly what `FlexKVRadixCache.evict` (`:454`) guards against with
  `_drain_completed_stores()` and `store_stream.synchronize()`.

So the hook must run before `cache_finished_req` for FlexKV, and would need to run after it for
LMCache.

### The ordering is already inconsistent today

FlexKV's requirement is not merely at risk of being broken by a future change — it is already
violated. Most sites call the abort hook first, e.g. `Scheduler.abort_chunked_req`:
```text
scheduler.py:3556   _release_aborted_request(req)
scheduler.py:3557   release_kv_cache(req, self.tree_cache, is_insert=False)
```

but two sites in `disaggregation/prefill.py` reverse it:
```text
prefill.py:1128   release_kv_cache(req, self.tree_cache)   # -> cache_finished_req, is_insert=True
prefill.py:1129   self._release_aborted_request(req)

prefill.py:1170   self.tree_cache.finish(req.cache_request_handle, CacheRequestOutcome.ABORT)
prefill.py:1172   release_kv_cache(req, self.tree_cache, is_insert=False)   # under holds_kv
```

With FlexKV as the tree cache, an abort on the `prefill.py:1128` path runs `cache_finished_req`
first — possibly registering an in-flight store in `_inflight_store_nodes` — and only then runs
`release_aborted_request`, which pops the registration and `dec_lock_ref`s a node whose store
has not completed. That is the sequence `evict()` is written to prevent.

Because the ordering is implicit — established by the order of two adjacent statements at each
of thirteen call sites, with nothing asserting it — there is no mechanism that keeps it correct.

## Design gap

The ordering conflict is a symptom of a broader lifecycle gap.

`release_aborted_request(handle)` is attempt-cancellation cleanup: it releases pending lookup,
prefetch, and other transient work left by an aborted attempt. Its docstring describes it that
way, and FlexKV's implementation matches — it cancels, and notifies nothing externally.
Cancellation does not mean the request has reached its final lifecycle boundary.

A hook with the right name and the right signature already exists:
```python
# base_prefix_cache.py:374
def finish(self, handle: CacheRequestHandle, outcome: CacheRequestOutcome) -> None:
    """Finish an attempt without cancelling successful asynchronous cache work."""
    if outcome != CacheRequestOutcome.SUCCESS:
        self.release_aborted_request(handle)
```

However, it is not currently used as a terminal lifecycle hook. `_release_aborted_request` is
itself nothing but a call to it:
```python
# scheduler.py:3310
def _release_aborted_request(self, req: Req) -> None:
    """Drop the cache-side state an aborted request left behind."""
    self.tree_cache.finish(req.cache_request_handle, CacheRequestOutcome.ABORT)
```

so the full path on every abort is:
```text
_release_aborted_request -> finish(ABORT) -> release_aborted_request
```

The scheduler invokes `finish` from the cancellation site, usually *before* `release_kv_cache`,
and the default implementation immediately translates that call back into cancellation.
Despite its name, `finish` therefore expresses early abort cancellation on these paths rather
than final request termination — the two semantics are not merely conflated by convention, they
are made equivalent by the base implementation itself.

`CacheRequestOutcome.SUCCESS`, meanwhile, has exactly one call site in the entire tree
(`disaggregation/prefill.py:1056`), and it reaches a body that does nothing. Terminal
finalization is instead effectively attached to `cache_finished_req`.

That is problematic because `cache_finished_req` represents KV-cache processing or write-back,
not request termination. `release_kv_cache` returns early before ever reaching it when the
request holds no KV cache:
```python
# common.py:283, in release_kv_cache
if not req.kv.holds_kv:
    ...                      # free mamba state, if any
    return                   # never reaches cache_finished_req (common.py:296)
```

This is not a corner case: the canonical leak window — an `AbortReq` for a request still in the
waiting queue — is precisely the state where the LMCache session has been opened by
`match_prefix` but no KV has been allocated yet. The most common leak path therefore does not
even reach the `release_kv_cache` fallback. Conversely, an aborted request that *does* hold KV
may still need to perform a final STORE before its session can be closed.

A third case shows the gap from the other side: `_clean_hicache_prefetch_resources`
(`decode_hicache_mixin.py:185`) calls `finish(..., ABORT)` only when
`decode_req.prefix_match.prefetch_registered` is true, so on that path an attempt can terminate
without the cache receiving any notification at all.

The missing contract is therefore:

> Every cache request attempt must receive exactly one terminal `finish(handle, outcome)`
> notification, after any required KV release or STORE, regardless of whether it ever held KV
> cache state and regardless of which abort path it took.

Cancellation and finalization must remain separate steps:
```text
cancel pending attempt work          (stays where it is today)
    -> optional release_kv_cache / cache_finished_req / STORE
    -> finish(handle, outcome)       (terminal, exactly once)
```

For paths where no KV finalization will occur, `finish` should run immediately after
cancellation. For paths that still perform a STORE, it should run afterwards.

**This cannot be done by moving the existing ****`finish(..., ABORT)`**** calls later.** Because the
default implementation forwards them to `release_aborted_request`, moving them past
`cache_finished_req` would delay FlexKV's cancellation and drop the lock of an in-flight store —
the exact failure described above, relocated to another backend. Abort cancellation has to stay
where it is and remain independently callable; only the terminal notification moves.

The encouraging part is that most of the wiring already exists: `finish` is already invoked on
all thirteen abort paths. What is missing is narrower than a full call-site audit:

1. the default implementation must stop equating `finish` with `release_aborted_request`, and
   the two phases must become separately callable;
2. `finish` must be invoked on successful completion paths as well — today `SUCCESS` reaches
   the cache from exactly one place;
3. on paths that perform a STORE, the terminal call must be positioned after it;
4. the conditional call in `_clean_hicache_prefetch_resources` must become unconditional.

A secondary observation: LMCache keys this state by `rid`, while the attempt lifecycle
introduced in #39318 is keyed by `CacheRequestHandle(rid, attempt_id)`. This is correct today
because the scheduler retires an attempt before starting the next, but it does not give LMCache
the attempt-level isolation FlexKV has.

## Related issues (searched, distinct)

- \#37160 — key isolation, not lifecycle
- \#34539 — store length, not lifecycle
- \#31445 — same class of problem, different backend and state; closed

### Reproduction

No single command reproduces the runtime leak; it needs an LMCache MP daemon plus an abort
landing in a specific window. Trigger conditions:

- LMCache enabled (`enable_lmcache`), MP mode (the default on non-XPU), i.e. `LMCRadixCache`
  is selected in `registry.py:116`;
- a request whose `match_prefix` reports `host_hit_length > 0`, so `_mp_match_prefix` records a
  marker and keeps the lookup locks (`lmc_radix_cache.py:231`);
- the request is aborted before `init_load_back` runs — e.g. `AbortReq` while it is still in
  the waiting queue (`scheduler.py:5429`), or `retire_unadmitted_request` (`:3239`).

The leak itself is directly reproducible in a unit test: drive `_mp_match_prefix` with a fake
connector that models the pending-lookup / read-lock bookkeeping, then call
`release_aborted_request` and observe that nothing is released. #40334 contains such a CPU-only
test (4 cases, no GPU and no `lmcache` install required).

Three paths are not covered yet: the disaggregated-decode ordering path (abort followed by
`cache_finished_req` and a STORE), the reversed ordering at `prefill.py:1128-1129` under
FlexKV, and the conditional notification in `_clean_hicache_prefetch_resources`.

### Environment

This report is based on code-path analysis and unit tests against `174a5f37b9`, not on an
observation from a production deployment. The machine below is the one used for that review; it
does not have `lmcache` installed, and the `sglang` version string below is its installed
package, not the commit analysed.

title: [Bug] /v1/responses drops the request priority
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`/v1/responses` accepts a `priority` field but never passes it to the engine: `create_responses` builds its `GenerateReqInput` without it. With `--enable-priority-scheduling`, every Responses request is scheduled as if it had no priority. Chat and completions pass it through fine.

Two related problems on the same path:

- `ResponsesRequest.priority` defaults to `0`, where the other request models default to `None`. Forwarding the field as is would send `0` for every request that sets nothing, which skips `--default-priority-value` and gets the request aborted under `--abort-on-priority-when-disabled`.
- The follow-up turns of built-in tool calls (`_generate_with_builtin_tools`) carry no priority either. The `priority = orig_priority - 1` at the end of that loop is never read.

Fix in #41087.

### Reproduction

We serve GLM-5.3-Flash with `--enable-priority-scheduling --schedule-low-priority-values-first`. A `/v1/responses` request sent with a priority is counted under `priority=""` in `sglang:num_requests_total`, while the same request on `/v1/chat/completions` is counted under the value it sent. With low values first, every Responses request ends up behind everything else in the queue.

The unit tests added in #41087 (`test_priority_forwarded_to_engine`, `test_tool_continuation_keeps_request_priority`) fail on `main` for the same reason.

### Environment

Seen on the `lmsysorg/sglang:glm-5.3-flash` image (`0.0.0.dev1+gfe236ea6c3.mmfix1`) on 8x H200, and still in the code on `main` (174a5f37b). I left out `check_env` since the bug is in request handling and doesn't depend on the hardware, but I can add it if needed.

title: [Bug] DWDP: expert weight copy peaks at 2x local expert memory, causing OOM at startup
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

DWDP setup peaks at **2x the local expert weight memory**, causing `cuMemCreate(local): 2` (`CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY`) at startup whenever a rank's expert shard fits once but not twice.

`_copy_local_weights_to_handles` (`python/sglang/srt/layers/moe/dwdp/transport.py`) copies each local expert weight into a new `cuMemCreate` block and frees the source with `untyped_storage().resize_(0)`. The freed memory stays in PyTorch's caching allocator, which `cuMemCreate` cannot use, and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` runs only once **after** the loop. So all source shards and all new blocks coexist until the end.

Estimated setup peak with the current code:

| Model | Config | Setup peak | GPU memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-120b | `--dwdp-size 2`, A100-40GB | ~61 GB | 40 GB (OOM) |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | `--dwdp-size 2`, A100-40GB | ~61 GB | 40 GB (OOM) |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B | `--dwdp-size 4`, B200 | ~235 GB | 180 GB (OOM) |


### Reproduction

No model needed: a single-GPU script that calls the real function. It leaves only 4 x 128 MiB of free device memory and copies 16 x 128 MiB shards. The models affected in practice are listed above.

`python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path openai/gpt-oss-20b --disable-flashinfer-autotune --dwdp-size 2 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --tp-size 2 --device cuda --host 127.0.0.1 --port 21010`

### Environment

DWDP code is identical between the tested checkout and main `1417345f5f`.

title: [Feature][DeepSeek-V4.1] Decode graph width is pinned to --context-length; add a decode-phase max_seq_len
body:
### TL;DR

On SM90, `--context-length` sets the decode indexer's **scan width**, not only the maximum servable context. The decode CUDA graph is captured with `max_seq_len = MAX_SEQ_LEN_FOR_CAPTURE = req_to_token.shape[1]`, and `PagedIndexerMetadata.max_compressed_seq_len` derives the indexer kernel's fixed column count from it. A deployment that actually serves 2K-token contexts therefore pays for a 1M-token scan on every decode step.

Measured, that is a **2.68x decode lever** — and it is not escapable from config: `PhaseConfig.max_seq_len` is accepted for `Phase.PREFILL` but not for `Phase.DECODE`, so the only way to collect it is to lower `--context-length` and give up long context.

PRs #39046 / #40431 / #40176 reduce the *work* done per capacity-sized tile, but they explicitly preserve the launch grid and the graph width. This is the complementary knob: let the decode graph be captured narrow, and fall back to eager for live contexts that exceed it — mirroring what prefill already does via `max_context_size` + `can_run_prefill_cuda_graph`.

### Environment

- 8 x H200, SM90 (sm_90), driver 570.211.01 / CUDA 12.8, all-to-all NV18
- `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-cu12-dsv41` @ `824bb45e1bf7486e49034bfa4bcad59aba799540`
- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (FP8 checkpoint; an md5-identical-config drop-in variant)
- `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4 --context-length 1048576 --max-running-requests 8 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 8 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.70 --schedule-policy lpm --moe-runner-backend humming --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 4 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 5`
- Replica B only; replica A's container id and `StartedAt` asserted unchanged across every recreate

### Measurement

Decode tok/s **per request**, median of 5 repeats, one unmeasured warm round. Per-request (not aggregate) so batch effects are removed.

| `--context-length` | indexer capacity (cols) | 2048 x1 | 2048 x8 | 65536 x8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1048576** (baseline) | 262144 | 98.4 | **32.1** | 35.31 |
| 524288 | 131072 | 128.01 | 49.41 | 52.55 |
| 262144 | 65536 | 131.51 | 67.93 | 73.59 |
| 131072 | 32768 | **147.93** | **85.98** | **88.0** |
| **gain, 1M -> 128K** | | **1.50x** | **2.68x** | **2.49x** |

Adjacent-tier 5-repeat ranges are disjoint everywhere (e.g. 65536 x8: `33.81-35.92`, `52.38-53.82`, `70.98-75.21`, `85.02-92.99`), against a measured run-to-run spread of 10-13%.

Cell labels are nominal: the harness over-calibrated and real prompt lengths are 2658 / 84261 tokens. Prompt construction is byte-identical across tiers and variants, so the overshoot is common mode and does not bias the deltas.

Three things identify the mechanism as a per-row fixed-width scan rather than a length- or weight-proportional cost:

1. **bs=1 gains 50% and saturates; bs=8 gains 168% and is still climbing.** The same capacity reduction is worth 8x more in absolute terms at bs=8 while the step it is charged against grows far more slowly.
2. **Cost is linear in capacity.** Inverting to step time at n=8: 31.15 / 20.24 / 14.72 ms for 262144 / 131072 / 65536 columns — halving the capacity halves the saving (10.91 : 5.52 = 1.98).
3. **A registered prediction.** Fitting `step_time(n=8) = 9.27 ms + 83.2 ns * capacity_columns` predicted ~83 tok/s at the 131072 tier before that tier was run; measured **85.98**.

Service-level effect: aggregate wall-clock throughput at 2048 x8 moves 226-247 -> 347-369 tok/s at the first tier alone (+50%), with TTFT flat to noise (0.438 -> 0.442 s) and the KV pool unchanged (-0.67% once, then flat).

Fresh-boot control excludes allocator/JIT state: after restoring the 1M config on a freshly booted replica the identical probe reproduces the baseline (102.7 / 32.16 / 35.6).

### Source (main)

- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsv4/metadata.py:322-324` — `max_compressed_seq_len` = `page_table.shape[1] * compressed_page_size`
- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsv4/indexer.py:1067` — that value is handed to the decode indexer as a fixed argument
- `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/deepseek_v4_backend.py:1214` — `MAX_SEQ_LEN_FOR_CAPTURE = self.req_to_token.shape[1]`; used for decode capture at `:2272-2298`
- `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/cuda_graph_config.py:78-88` — `ALLOWED_KEYS_PER_PHASE[Phase.DECODE]` has no `max_seq_len`; `Phase.PREFILL` has it (plus `max_context_size`)
- prefill already has the fallback this request wants for decode: `deepseek_v4_backend.py:1557-1559` (cap `num_pages` by the graph width) and `:1586-1592` (`can_run_prefill_cuda_graph`)

### Negative control

The identical `--max-model-len` change on vLLM, same box, same checkpoint, moves aggregate throughput by 3.6-4.9% (2048 x8: 1102.8 -> 1142.5; 65536 x8: 829.2 -> 869.9). vLLM's static launch shape with a per-row `[start, end)` loop has no such coupling, which rules out "this is the unavoidable price of sparse attention at 1M".

### What the lever costs today

Against 12h of production traffic, `--context-length=262144` rejects at most 1 request in 5005 (`#cached-token` p99.9 = 199,936 tokens, a 31% margin) while more than doubling decode at the concurrency production actually runs at. But 131072 is another 27% on top and cuts below p99.9 — a capability decision — and 1M becomes unreachable either way.

### Proposal

1. accept `"max_seq_len"` in `ALLOWED_KEYS_PER_PHASE[Phase.DECODE]`;
2. use it as `max_seq_len` for decode graph capture and decode metadata in place of `MAX_SEQ_LEN_FOR_CAPTURE`;
3. replay a decode batch eagerly when its live max sequence length exceeds it (mirror `can_run_prefill_cuda_graph`).

One caveat worth stating up front: the capture width cannot vary per batch, so a naive clamp inside the kernel would be *worse* than the flag — a clamped graph would silently ignore the tail of a longer sequence instead of rejecting it. A decode-only `max_seq_len` needs the same explicit eager fallback prefill has.

### Ask

Is this the intended direction, or is the plan to let #40431 / #40176 absorb the coupling at the kernel level? If the former, I am happy to prototype the config plumbing.

---

*Independent of #40431: that PR makes invisible tiles cheap while keeping the grid; this changes how many tiles exist and lets a 1M-context deployment capture a 128K decode graph.*

title: [Feature][Spec][XPU] Honor rejection sampling in EAGLE chain verification
body:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

EAGLE verification on XPU takes the greedy argmax path even when the batch is non-greedy and --speculative-use-rejection-sampling is enabled. For a configuration that passes the startup checks, the startup hook reports rejection sampling as enabled, but the XPU verification gate still prevents that sampler from being reached.

I would like to enable the existing chain-rejection path on XPU, subject to hardware validation and coordination with related work.

Current behavior

Source snapshot: 32290dda2cea4bb95274b3d08e43d4dad74e9676.

In python/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_utils.py, _verify_uses_greedy() returns:

return is_all_greedy or is_cpu or is_xpu or (
    is_hip and not use_rejection_sampling
)

The unconditional is_xpu term selects the branch containing torch.argmax(next_token_logits, dim=-1), including when is_all_greedy=False and use_rejection_sampling=True.

Meanwhile, speculative_hook.py logs:

Rejection sampling is enabled for speculative decoding (speculative_use_rejection_sampling=True).

The issue is therefore a mismatch between the enabled configuration and the verification path actually selected.

This is a source-level finding. I have not yet reproduced the behavior or validated an alternative on XPU hardware. The ignored flag was also noted as a side issue in #35144.

Proposed scope

Allow non-greedy XPU batches with rejection sampling explicitly enabled to reach chain_speculative_sampling_triton.

The existing startup checks and sampling-branch validation would remain unchanged:

The resolved algorithm must be EAGLE or EAGLE3, including NEXTN configurations that resolve to EAGLE.

--speculative-eagle-topk must be 1.

Both acceptance thresholds must be 1.0, and deterministic inference must be disabled.

Draft proposal probabilities must be present and use the target vocabulary.

These are inherited requirements of the existing rejection-sampling path, not additional XPU-specific restrictions. The speculative branching factor is separate from request-level sampling top_k.

Automatic enablement and the separate target-only stochastic tree-verification path are outside this proposal. Greedy requests and other backends should retain their existing behavior.

Related implementation work

#37134 provides a reference for enabling the Triton chain-rejection path on ROCm.

intel/llm-scaler#719, merged September 17, 2026, implements out-of-tree target-only stochastic XPU verification using SYCL/PyTorch operations and a patch to eagle_info_v2.py. It addresses the broader XPU sampling limitation, but is distinct from enabling the existing Triton chain sampler with actual draft proposal probabilities.

#34140 is also related to the separate target-only tree path on ROCm. I would like to coordinate with these efforts rather than duplicate planned upstream work.

Implementation considerations

Once XPU reaches the rejection-sampling branch, the existing renormalization dispatch already imports top_k_renorm_prob and top_p_renorm_prob from sgl_kernel.

The XPU dependency file pins sglang-kernel-xpu 0.2.0. I would first verify that this pinned wheel exposes working versions of the required operations and validate their cutoff and tie semantics against the intended sampling behavior. Related XPU sampler integration: #38510.

The Triton/PyTorch renormalization fallback is an alternative, not the existing XPU route. Using it would require explicit dispatch changes and an XPU-compatible _prepare_probs guard.

The sampling branch also broadcasts verification results across tensor-parallel ranks. TP > 1 therefore needs explicit validation in light of #35144/#35195; enabling the gate alone would not establish multi-XPU correctness.

Validation

Validation should include:

Gate-routing and configuration regression tests, including unchanged greedy behavior and the existing unsupported-configuration checks.

Actual XPU chain-sampler and renormalization tests against independent references, covering acceptance, rejection, all-drafts-accepted sampling, and top-k/top-p boundary and tie cases.

End-to-end non-greedy and mixed greedy/non-greedy batches, with distributional checks rather than output diversity or task accuracy alone.

Graph capture enabled/disabled and TP=1/TP>1 where supported, preserving and testing the existing draft_probs copy after graph replay so the proposal probabilities remain intact until verification.

Maintainer input

Is there an upstreaming plan for intel/llm-scaler#719 or another XPU verification effort that this should coordinate with? Would a focused in-tree chain-rejection enablement PR be useful alongside the target-only work?

I do not currently have guaranteed XPU hardware access. Before committing to an implementation, I would appreciate guidance on the preferred approach and whether hardware validation could be coordinated with an XPU contributor.

### Related resources

_No response_

title: [Bug] DFLASH draft layout is assumed, not validated: anchor-first checkpoints shift every position silently
body:
# [Bug] DFLASH draft layout is assumed, not validated: anchor-first checkpoints shift every position silently

### Summary

`DFLASH` draft checkpoints carry an implicit block-layout convention, and SGLang assumes
one of the two conventions in common use without checking which one a checkpoint was
trained with. A checkpoint trained with the *anchor-as-first-prediction* layout — where
every position in the block predicts — is served without any error and produces draft
tokens shifted by one position. The server reports healthy; acceptance collapses to
roughly `1.0` (only the anchor/bonus token survives).

Isolated on a Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (`Qwen4Exp`) target with the official DeepSpec drafter
`dflash_block7_qwen38_flash_next` on 8×A800 (SM80): **accept length @ 4-token window =
1.0621** over 47,411 verify steps. The same checkpoint's card reports a *served* accepted
length of **2.7562 at block 4** and **2.9837 at its native block 7** under vLLM, where the
layout it was trained for is honoured. No warning, no assertion here — the service starts
and answers normally, at a fraction of that acceptance.

### The two conventions

| | anchor-as-first-prediction | 1+N (SGLang's assumption) |
|---|---|---|
| block positions | all `K` positions predict | position 0 is the seeded anchor/bonus token; positions `1..N` are the drafts |
| marker, when present | `sample_from_anchor: true` | `sample_from_anchor: false` |
| drafter | DeepSpec `dflash_block7_qwen38_flash_next` | speculators-format drafts |

The marker is a **speculators** config field (`DFlashSpeculatorConfig.sample_from_anchor`,
default `False`; `DSparkSpeculatorConfig` defaults `True`). The convention also determines the
token count: `False` → `block_size - 1` speculative tokens, `True` → `block_size`.

**It is not a reliable discriminator across the ecosystem, which is part of the problem.**
The official anchor-first checkpoint above carries **no `sample_from_anchor` field at all** —
neither top-level nor inside its `dflash_config`; its config exposes `num_anchors: 512` and
nothing else about the layout. So a marker-based check would read the sglang default and wave
exactly the checkpoint that mis-serves through.

**But the layout *is* declared — under a name SGLang does not read.** The upstream serving repo
ships a config override (the README notes the checkpoint's own `config.json` "does not carry the
`dflash_config` block the engine reads"). That override's `dflash_config` contains:

```json
"dflash_config": {
  "target_layer_ids": [3, 15, 23, 35, 43],
  "mask_token_id": 248077,
  "use_aux_hidden_state": true,
  "causal": false,
  "query_zero_predicts_next": true
}
```

`query_zero_predicts_next: true` is a direct, explicit statement of the anchor-first convention.
SGLang's `DFlashDraftConfig` (`speculative/dflash_utils.py:529-548`) has no field for it and
`parse_dflash_draft_config` never reads it — a tree-wide search for the identifier returns zero
hits. So the declaration exists, is unambiguous, and is silently dropped.

> **Inference, not a confirmed contract.** I am reading `query_zero_predicts_next` as "the
> query at position 0 predicts the token *after* the anchor", i.e. the anchor-first layout —
> that is what the field name says and it is consistent with the extra `block_size`-th
> prediction the layout implies, but I have not verified it against the trainer source and am
> labelling it as a hypothesis rather than a spec. If the maintainers confirm the field's
> meaning, a check on it is the natural fix; if not, the layout still has to be established
> some other way. It should not be shipped as a hard gate on my reading alone.

### Where SGLang assumes 1+N

`DFlashWorkerV2` slices the draft's hidden states to drop position 0:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/speculative/dflash_worker_v2.py:158-160
# draft tokens are block positions 1: (pos 0 is the seeded bonus token)
bs = hidden_states.shape[0] // self.block_size
hs = hidden_states.view(bs, self.block_size, -1)[:, 1:, :].reshape(
    -1, hidden_states.shape[-1]
)
```

The same slice appears in the in-worker draft path (`dflash_worker_v2.py:278`,
`# pos 0 = anchor`) and in the selector path (`:1378`, `:2572`).

A checkpoint trained anchor-first produces `K` meaningful predictions per block, but only
`K-1` of them are read, and each one is read from the *wrong* slot — a uniform off-by-one
across every draft position.

### The layout field is already parsed — just not for this

`dflash_utils.py` already reads `sample_from_anchor` off the draft config:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/speculative/dflash_utils.py:504-507
sample_from_anchor = dflash_config.get(
    "sample_from_anchor", _cfg_get(config, "sample_from_anchor", True)
)
return sample_from_anchor is False
```

Two things follow from that snippet. First, the field is already parsed at config-parse time.
Second, **its default is inverted for this purpose**: `_cfg_get(..., True)` reads the sglang
default as `True`, but the speculators default for the DFlash family is `False`. So "absent"
means *opposite* things to the two sides, which is why absence cannot be treated as safety.

Today the read is confined to `is_nemotron_35_draft_config` (`dflash_utils.py:470`), and even
there it is one of six conjunctive conditions identifying one specific published checkpoint —
it is not a general layout gate. The value is available on the DFLASH path and simply not
consulted there.

### Suggested fix (fail fast, matching vLLM)

vLLM's DFlash speculator raises on this exact layout
(`ValueError: sample_from_anchor=True is not supported for DFlash`). SGLang currently does
something worse than raising: it serves, silently, at ~1.0 acceptance.

Three options, in increasing order of how much they depend on my unverified reading above:

1. **Minimal, no inference needed for the check itself:** fail fast on the checkpoints that *do*
   declare a layout — anything SGLang can currently see (`sample_from_anchor` where present).
   Wiring up `query_zero_predicts_next` would extend this to the official checkpoint, but **that
   rests on my unverified reading of the field (hypothesis, see above) — it should only be
   treated as a gate once the semantics are confirmed.** As it stands this option would not have
   caught the official checkpoint, because SGLang reads neither field today; it is a strict
   improvement over the current state and commits to nothing uncertain.
2. **Require an explicit declaration** on the DFLASH draft config going forward, and refuse to
   serve a checkpoint that omits it. Catches everything, including this checkpoint — at the
   cost of breaking checkpoints that are in the wild today.
3. **Honour the layout** — read all `K` positions when the checkpoint is anchor-first. The most
   useful outcome, and a bounded change at the four slice sites above, but it is downstream of
   the layout actually being established.

Either way the checkpoint stops being served at a wrong-but-plausible acceptance rate.

The design constraint worth flagging: **an explicit check on `sample_from_anchor` alone would
not have caught this checkpoint** — it declares neither that field nor `speculative_tokens`
(the identifier does not appear anywhere in its config). Whatever is chosen has to *establish*
the layout rather than default it.

Two things I'd be glad to be corrected on: whether `query_zero_predicts_next` means what I read
it to mean, and whether there is a better discriminator for layout than anything proposed here
— I've only looked at one checkpoint family and would rather defer to the maintainers than guess.

### Reproduction

**Prerequisite:** this needs the Qwen4-Exp capture guard from **#38642** (rebased onto current
main). On bare main the Qwen4-Exp DFLASH path never reaches the draft at all — the server dies
during decode CUDA-graph capture (`ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)`, see
#38589). With the guard, the server comes up and the numbers below reproduce.

SM80 (8×A800), main + #38642, official DeepSpec drafter, `--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4`:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <Qwen3.8-Flash-Next target> \
  --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
  --speculative-draft-model-path <DFlash2 draft, block 4, 24 heads, taps [1,7,14,20,26,32,39,45]> \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 --tp 8 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 8 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
```
(8xA800 SM80, driver 550.144.03, torch 2.11.0+cu130. On SM80 the tilelang/nvcc header
check also needs `NVCC_PREPEND_FLAGS=-DCCCL_DISABLE_CTK_COMPATIBILITY_CHECK`.)

Note that `--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4` is not a free choice here: Qwen4-Exp's QSA
caps the window at its compression ratio
(`layers/attention/qwen_sparse_attn_backend.py:240`, `_require_chain_speculation`), so a
`block_size=7` checkpoint cannot even be launched at its training block size.

### Measured acceptance (4-token window)

| concurrency | requests | failures | accept length | accept rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 300 | 0 | **1.0621** | 0.0184 |
| 24 | 300 | 0 | 1.0643 | 0.0190 |
| 48 | 300 | 0 | 1.0629 | 0.0186 |

An earlier independent run at concurrency 8 gave 1.0604 (47,377 steps), i.e. run-to-run spread
at fixed concurrency is ~0.002.

Per-position, pooled over 47,411 verify steps (concurrency 8):

| position k | P(accept at k \| prefix matched) | P(accept length ≥ k) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0497 | 0.0497 |
| 2 | 0.1024 | 0.0051 |
| 3 | 0.3485 | 0.0018 |

95.0% of verify steps accept **zero** draft tokens; the bottleneck is position 1. The
6×-concurrency sweep moves accept length by <0.4%, so this is steady-state behaviour, not
a load artifact.

### Related

- #38589 — the sibling report on this target: Qwen4Exp cannot emit DFlash aux hidden
  states at all. That is a prerequisite failure; this one is what remains once a drafter
  *can* be served.
- Same shape of problem, one layer down: the block-size mismatch between a draft's training
  `block_size` and the served `--speculative-num-draft-tokens` is warned about
  (`dflash_worker_v2.py:468`) and then silently forced (`:472`). DFLASH's convolution
  indexes by `position % block_size`, so a mismatch shifts positions too. Fail-fast there
  would have caught this class of problem earlier.

Happy to test either fix on the SM80 rig.
